* fix(vault): the identifier-interval scenario retires after valid_from, not a fixed hour (#996)

The R20(e) scenario file was red on d96172c40 and carried as pre-existing by
the three wave 0b receipt sections. The primary-preference partial index and
the interval CHECK both survived e03345d6c's fold intact — a freshly
bootstrapped vault reports them exactly as schema/core.ts writes them, and no
DDL changes here.

What failed was the retirement, not the replacement: core.add_party stamps
valid_from from the gateway's wall clock, while the scenario end-dated the row
at a fixed 2026-09-06T10:00:00.000Z. R20(e)'s own invariant then refuses the
update for every run starting after that hour — green when the file was
written, red for every run since. The scenario now retires at one instant
derived from the clock of the run, shared by every assertion in the file.

* feat(vault): one invariant boundary — domain operations every writer passes through (#996)

Domain commands, imports and Atlas each enforced a different subset of the
model. `people.add_important_date` refused February 31 and `atlas.insert_row`
wrote it; nothing anywhere refused `due_at: "banana"`; a task could be its own
parent. `packages/vault/src/operations/` is now the one place a canonical write
means something, and Atlas's shared pre/postconditions are the operations' —
the writer matrix refuses every invalid mutation through every writer with the
same sentence.

Simple invariants moved into the schema, so they hold for the seat's local
apply too: a readable due_at, a real month-day, a hex sha256, and triggers for
the acyclic hierarchy, section/project agreement and a hash that cannot change
while its bytes stay put. Two columns join them — a recurring task's series
identity, and an imported rule's explicit support state.

Completion became one operation shared by People, Tasks and automations, so a
successor inherits the series and the person it is about; `people.toggle_task`
is deleted. The occurrence key became one typed value in `packages/core/src/
time/occurrence.ts`: the readers named a column that did not exist, and under
that the matcher keyed on the resolved instant while the writer stored the
series-local wall clock, so a zoned skip matched nothing either way. Concept
identity stops falling back to the ASCII slug, an account stops being selected
by its display label, and an intent that names its operation must reference
every row that operation read.

* feat(tally): money keeps its currency — balances, valuations and the export (#996)

`pairwise` folded minor units into a map keyed by party alone and the
dashboard labelled the sum with the vault's base currency, so a friend you
owed EUR 100 and USD 100 read as one 200 — a figure true in neither money, on
the app's most-read screen. Every currency it needed had been in the DDL since
#916 and every one of them was read past.

`Money` is amount plus currency, and adding two currencies throws rather than
producing a third number. A position that spans currencies is a bag of
amounts; a single figure over one is a valuation that either names the rates
it used or says it is unavailable and shows the components — there is no rate
plane in the product, and inventing one was the defect.

The output contract moved with it, so a bare number is unrenderable as a
balance and all 134 call sites came from the compiler rather than from a grep:
per-friend balances, each group's own money, a member's net, a part, a
proposed transfer and the two hero totals. Settlements, obligations and the
export use the same helpers — the export was shipping the base currency on a
group's own ledger, into a file that outlives the app.

* feat(vault): claims carry their evidence, deletion carries its role (#996)

Wave 0e of #996. A machine tag now names the derivation and the input revision
behind it, and `core_tag`'s table-level UNIQUE — which made two engine profiles
disagreeing unrepresentable — is replaced by one partial index per asserter: an
owner's assertion, and one row per derivation. Which claim READS as the answer
is derived (owner, then the policy's profile, then the built-in engines, then a
stable tie-break) and stored nowhere.

Deletion is declared by relationship role beside every reference onto a person
or a content item: 56 declarations over five roles, each carrying its reason,
with the role fixing the ON DELETE rule and the purge behaviour tested per role.

The thirteen scenarios #996 was opened over stop being thirteen tests and become
a scripted fixture — real commands against a fresh vault on a repeatable clock
and id sequence, every claim read back through a surface's own read path, and
each naming the two app surfaces its round trip crosses. It is exported as
`@centraid/vault/tests/ontology-scenarios` so W1's convergence run replays it.

Carried in: the client FTS parity fix (the representation split made the content
title an expression over `media_asset`, and no shape ships it), red on the tree
this wave started from.

governance: allow-toolchain-config the vault's test tsconfig and vitest config
gain `tests/**` (and `rootDir: "."`, since the fixture ships as source beside
the package rather than inside its build) so the scripted scenario fixture is
typechecked and run by the package's own scripts. Nothing is relaxed: the
fixture is held to exactly the settings `src` is held to.

* feat(vault): the seat's shape — private tables, split identity, row_version, the log (#996)

What a seat may hold becomes a table list rather than a per-app shape, the key
material two identity registers carried moves a table away instead of being
excluded column by column, every mutable row gains the version an intent's
conflict check compares, and `replica_log` exists with its two numbers.

- `schema/private-tables.ts`: 24 declarations in three kinds, each with its
  reason, plus the property the list exists for as a function — no replicated
  table keys into a private one, which is what lets a seat run with foreign
  keys off and still satisfy the constraints the gateway committed under.
- `access_device` / `access_agent` split (R3): the identity projection
  replicates so `origin_device_id` and `camera_device_id` resolve on a seat;
  `access_device_secret` and `access_agent_secret` hold the rest. The private
  sibling references the replicated parent, never the reverse.
- `row_version` on 67 mutable tables (R6), bumped by the same touch trigger.
  The WHEN guard moved to `row_version`, so a writer that stamps `updated_at`
  by hand no longer skips the bump.
- `replica_log` (R5) with `commit_seq`, `schema_epoch` and `ddl_version` as
  separate columns, `pk_json`, `row_json`, `indirect` and `producer`.
- One `schema_epoch` bump for waves 0b and 1; golden corpus re-frozen.
- `SEAT_SQLITE_FLOOR = 3.49.1`: the phone, not the gateway, is the oldest
  build, and nothing here is newer than it.

* feat(vault): the log has a producer — session capture, the decoder, the oracle (#996)

A commit stops being something the schema reports through triggers it has to
regenerate, and becomes something SQLite already knows and the gateway asks it
for. One session per replicated table, opened and decoded inside the caller's
transaction, so the mutation and its log rows commit together or not at all.

- `core/protocol/row-json.ts`: BLOBs as base64, integers past 2^53 as decimal
  strings, SQL NULL as `null`, an absent column as an absent key — the three
  values a photo vault holds that JSON silently loses. Base64 by hand: the
  package is dependency-free and the code runs on all three seats.
- `replica/changeset.ts`: the v1 wire format, because `node:sqlite` exposes
  `changeset()` and `applyChangeset()` and no iterator between them. Integers
  read as bigint, not Number.
- `replica/log.ts`: the capture and the decoder. One session per table is
  mandatory, not tidy — `createSession({ filter })` is accepted and silently
  ignored, so a filtered session would carry the private tables it was told to
  skip. An UPDATE changeset omits untouched columns, so each touched row is
  read back by the changeset's own key flags, inside the transaction.
- `replica/apply.ts`: `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`, one transaction per
  commit with the cursor in it, an epoch gate that refuses rather than skips.
  It ships now because a convergence gate without an applier is a test of the
  test.
- `replica/log.test.ts`: seventeen cases in three batteries — capture and
  decode, the oracle against native `applyChangeset`, convergence over EVERY
  replicated table plus FTS query parity, duplicate delivery and crash
  mid-batch.

* feat(vault): the sanitised seat snapshot, the two doors, and a canary over bytes (#996)

A seat bootstraps by being handed the file. What makes that safe is not what
the copy contains but what has been physically removed from it — and the test
for that reads the bytes, never the catalog.

- `replica/seat-snapshot.ts`: P4 variant B end to end — `VACUUM INTO`, then
  `secure_delete=ON` on the copy BEFORE any drop, every trigger but FTS sync,
  every index and view naming a private table, the private tables, both log
  truncations leaving `floor_seq` as the seat's resume cursor, and the final
  `VACUUM` that actually reclaims the pages.
- The canary is planted in a private table with a replicated parent, asserted
  present in an unsanitised copy first and absent from the snapshot's bytes.
  The seat file is opened raw: no migration ladder, no app-defined function,
  no trigger regeneration. A snapshot that needed those would not be one.
- `namesPrivateTable` strips SQL comments: the first run dropped a live index
  because the table's DDL explains its private neighbour in prose.
- `golden-snapshot.ts`'s FTS exclusion was `NOT LIKE '%_fts%'`, where `_` is
  LIKE's one-character wildcard — it excluded nothing, and the frozen manifest
  carried 51 index tables against 17 real ones. Now 17.
- Route contract for the snapshot, log-tail and locker-key doors, with two
  optional capability flags that ship `false` until the handlers exist.
- Ledger row `gateway/snapshot/year3`: 106,233,856 → 64,569,344 B raw,
  9,145,212 B gzipped, 2,261/2,326 ms, 25 private tables and 554 objects
  dropped. Both log truncations are a third of the file.

* feat(vault): the retention floor, the producer bound, and the deferral flag (#996)

Compaction is gone. The old change log folded superseded entries because a
change entry was a pointer — "row X changed" — and several for one row said
nothing the last one did. A log row is a full image, so folding buys nothing a
truncation does not, and it cost a prior-op pair on every row.

- `pruneReplicaLog`: a floor that may not cross a commit edge (a seat resuming
  there would get half a transaction) and may not cross a live seat's cursor
  (OQ-13 — pruning past a phone converts a cheap tail into a forced
  re-bootstrap, silently, on the gateway's schedule rather than the member's).
  The seat cursor is a hold, not a hint: it defaults on rather than needing to
  be passed.
- `REPLICA_PRODUCER_MAX_ROWS = 2000`, confirmed against P2's measurements: at
  most 1.4 MB of row_json and ~38 KB gzip-6, under 4% of the threshold, so a
  conforming producer cannot produce a deferrable commit by accident.
- `REPLICA_DEFER_THRESHOLD_BYTES = 1_000_000`, in COMPRESSED bytes and never
  in rows: the same 10,000-row commit measures 55 KB, 209 KB or 184 KB
  gzipped depending on op, a 6.6x spread.
- `replica_log.deferred`: one verdict per commit on every row of it, because a
  commit is the unit a seat applies and so the unit it defers. A conforming
  commit is never compressed to find out.
- Ledger row `gateway/log-apply/1000-commits`: 10,000 rows in 3,878.6 ms —
  2,578 rows/s, 258 commits/s. Transaction-bound, not row-bound, which is the
  price of the cursor riding in the commit it stands for.

* feat(server): the seat doors, and an index no function can pin (#996)

A seat needs exactly two things from the gateway: the file, once, and the log,
forever after. Both are served now, and the search index stops being something
only the gateway can maintain.

- `seat-routes.ts`, mounted ahead of the shaped route's prefixes, on the same
  `resolveReplicaAccess` identity: a seat is an enrolled device, and the
  question these doors answer is "is this an enrolled seat", never "which rows
  may it see".
- The snapshot door is a STATIC FILE, not an RPC. At year-3 volume the
  artifact is ~64 MB and the client is a phone on a train; a file gets ranges,
  a strong ETag and conditional requests from the transport, and it is
  immutable for its name because it is a pure function of the log position it
  stands at. Compressed on disk and served as those bytes — `Content-Encoding`
  would quietly make a byte range a range over something else.
- The log door serves WHOLE COMMITS: `?since=&limit=`, bounded, the page
  carrying the rest of its last commit whatever the limit says. A stale cursor
  is 409 `seat_rebootstrap_required` naming the floor, the watermark and the
  snapshot route. The epoch gate runs on every ROW, not only the cursor: the
  cursor check is about the request, the row check is about the answer.
- The `K` door authenticates and then says it has nothing —
  `seat_locker_key_unavailable`, deliberately not the 404 an unrouted path
  gives, because a seat must tell "no locker key here" from "gateway too old".
  W6 fills it in.
- `vault_content_text` is retired: the decode moved to write time in
  `setRepresentation`, the FTS triggers read `core_content_text.body_text`, and
  the same trigger text now runs on a phone that cannot register a SQL
  function. The decoder moved out of `schema/fts.ts` with it — the index reads
  a column now, so it was never an FTS concern.
- `declared-writes.conformance` caught what a reviewer would not: eleven
  actions across seven blueprints now write `core.content_text` and had to say
  so. `tests/quality/backup-corpus-fixture.ts` carried two reds this umbrella
  had left there — a seed still writing the dropped `media_type`/`title`, and
  a determinism case failing on wall-clock residue in pages `canonicalize`
  frees. Both fixed, never the gate.

* feat(vault): the outcome contract — where it landed, and what it waits on (#996)

An intent was answered and forgotten. Five things it never told anyone are now
durable: where it landed, what it produced, what it is waiting for, how long
its answer is good for, and what to do when that runs out.

- `commit_seq` and the produced `(table, pk, row_version)` set are stamped at
  the GROUP-COMMIT boundary, inside the canonical transaction. That is the
  seam because the gateway batches invocations into one transaction: the
  position and the produced rows belong to the BATCH. The set is read from the
  capture's decoded images, never re-queried — a second read could see a later
  commit's value and settle the intent against work it did not do.
- Both doors, one stamp. The member door now RECORDS an outcome before
  invoking; it previously answered from the invoke result and kept nothing, so
  a lost acknowledgement had nothing to replay against.
- The conflict check moved onto `row_version`. `MAX(seq)` over `replica_change`
  is a property of the TRANSPORT — it moves when the log is pruned or the epoch
  bumped, and a seat holding `vault.db` whole cannot compute it at all.
  `row_version` is on the row and means the same thing on both.
- `dependsOn` makes the chain causal at the gateway, which is the only place
  that sees the whole chain. Three verdicts, not two: waiting releases itself
  when the predecessor lands, abandoned never will, and naming the predecessor
  is the difference between a queue that drains and one that quietly stops. A
  chain park re-enters dispatch — unlike a park that waits on a PERSON.
- Predecessor references resolve by plain equality from the outcome table,
  never "the latest". Which produced row is not guessed: the placeholder names
  its table, or exactly one row survives after the engine's own bookkeeping —
  otherwise it is left unresolved so the command refuses loudly.
- The idempotency window is thirty days, the same number as the retention
  floor on purpose, and an outcome is never pruned while a seat's cursor is
  behind it. Past the window the answer is "I no longer know" with an explicit
  recovery; the same id with a different payload is refused. Neither
  re-executes.

* feat(client): the seat takes the file and the log — applier, bootstrap (#996)

Wave 1 served the file once and the log forever after. This is the other end
of both.

THE APPLIER, IN FOUR RULES. One commit, one transaction, cursor included, so a
crash leaves a boundary the next attempt resumes from. `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`
and never REPLACE, which deletes first and desynchronises the only triggers a
seat keeps. Idempotent by seq, proven by a delete followed by the same page
redelivered. Foreign keys off, because a page can carry a child before its
parent's commit and the gateway's integrity is the only integrity.

AND ONE REFUSAL. A row from another schema epoch is caught before the first
transaction opens and refuses the page WHOLE — applying what came before it
leaves a cursor naming a file the seat no longer has, which is the state
re-bootstrap exists to avoid.

THE BOOTSTRAP IS A RESUMABLE DOWNLOAD. Resume by byte range pinned to the
door's ETag; a staged prefix of another artifact is discarded, never spliced.
Room for the current file, the artifact and the expanded copy is checked
before the first byte, against a measured 7.26x expansion. FTS is rebuilt
after the copy, from the file's own schema, so a broken index fails there
rather than on the member's first search.

The wire both ends read moves into `packages/core`; the door's answers are
typed by it. The worker is host-neutral, so the browser and the suites run the
same program. Parity is the gate: same SQL, two files, over the 0e fixture
with a real tail applied and over the year-3 vault.

Two reds found on the way and fixed here: the year-3 fixture cache was serving
a pre-#996 artifact because the ladder length does not move when the baseline
is rewritten, and year-3 notes were not searchable because the seeder never
wrote the decoded-text row wave 1's triggers now read.

* feat(vault): membership is state — the closure predicate and three outputs (#996)

A share stops being a composed shape and becomes what R10 says it is: the
same log under a closure predicate, with membership as explicit state. The
transport that ships is untouched and green — `composeShareShape` still
serves every subscription — because the share transport is never deleted
before its replacement lands.

- THE GRANT IS THE SHAPE. `shape_id` leaves both subscription tables for
  `authority_id`; `share_subscription`'s key becomes
  `(authority_id, audience_vault_id)`, the lineage's becomes
  `(authority_id, target_type, target_id)`, and the separate `grant_id`
  column and its index go. The `@share:` sigil survives only where it is a
  wire value, resolved to the grant at the peer door.
- MEMBERSHIP, ON THE ORIGIN. `share_subscription_member(authority_id,
  table_name, pk, entered_seq)` plus `INDEX (table_name, pk)` for "which
  live grants claim this row". `pk` IS `replica_log.pk_json`, so a member
  row and a log row join by equality and a composite key needs no second
  column; a retained row keeps its `entered_seq`, which is what makes a
  reconnect after retention expiry a resend rather than a re-bootstrap.
- THE THREE OUTPUTS. `enter` from the member-set diff — measured here, an
  existing photograph added to a shared album writes two log rows and moves
  four rows into scope, so the log alone can never answer it. `update` from
  the log, coalesced by `(table, pk)`, because one field edit writes two log
  rows. `leave` from the diff in reverse, for rows that did not themselves
  change and for the purged member no revocation covers.
- DERIVED ROWS NEVER PROJECT, BY TABLE. `core_content_derivative` and
  `core_content_text` leave the closure, `projectDerivatives` is deleted,
  and derived bytes leave the blob manifest with it. What crossed the
  boundary — a generated caption, an OCR pass, a transcript, an embedding, a
  thumbnail — is now enqueued as the recipient's own work under the
  recipient's own egress answers.

Exit criterion: every live subscription of the generated year-3 vault
converges under the predicate across all three outputs.

* feat(client): bytes, seat state, and a fixture that stopped being a slice (#996)

The applier gave a seat the vault's rows. This is everything else it holds.

BYTES. A thumb is a ROW — it arrives with the vault and no policy governs it,
and the byte policy refuses to answer about one rather than let that confusion
reach a screen that waits on a fetch nothing needed. What is negotiable is the
files, under three policies, with two overrides that are promises already
made: a pin, and a capture the member's own queued work needs (R25).

A PURGE IS A HANDSHAKE. `seat_blob_presence` keeps its row through the
tombstone and through the acknowledgement, because "I have forgotten about
this blob" and "I never had it" must not be the same answer — without the
difference the gateway cannot tell every seat dropping a blob from one seat
being offline for a month.

THE STORAGE PROBE (OQ-2) decides full or rows-minus-FTS from the quota rather
than from a browser name, refuses instead of inventing a third contents, and
drops the FTS tables together with the sync triggers — the seat-side step wave
1 named when it declined to drop them in the snapshot pipeline.

THE CARRY-OVER COMES OUT BEFORE THE SWAP. Queued intents, held blobs and pins
exist nowhere but the file a re-bootstrap is about to replace, and unlike every
row in it none of them can be re-fetched. `created_order` is carried verbatim:
a repair that renumbers the queue re-orders the member's work.

THE SEAT WATERMARK replaces the custody line's census record count — under R1
every seat holds the same rows, so the number said nothing about the machine
it was printed beside.

And the golden replica stops being a slice: it is the gateway's sanitised file
plus a real log tail, with "never hand-built" now an assertion that fails at
build time rather than a comment.

Three reds fixed on the way: the journey ledger had an undeclared volume, a
shared blueprint file carried two raw NUL bytes, and this receipt's wave-1 file
list named files by basename where the gate needs full paths.

* feat(vault): the tail door, and an audience that applies rows (#996)

The predicate has a transport. An origin door serves the three outputs since
an audience's cursor; the audience applies them as ROWS re-keyed through
lineage. Both stand BESIDE `composeShareShape`, which goes in the next commit
once the convergence gate has passed through this one.

- THE DOOR. `composeShareTail` returns a pass — the frame to send and the
  `settle` that makes its membership durable — kept apart so a failed
  delivery retries against the same `before` set. Mounted at
  `/centraid/_peer/replica/tail` under the same link-pair admission as every
  other door on the plane. A cursor is a CLAIM, not an acknowledgement: the
